title: MCA Widens Its Overseas Listing Route Beyond Plain Equity Shares to Convertible Debentures and Preference Shares
meta_description: MCA's 3 November 2026 amendment lets Indian firms list convertible debentures and preference shares abroad, not just equity shares, with a QIB condition.
case_name: Companies (Listing of Equity Instruments in Permissible Jurisdictions) Amendment Rules, 2026
citation: G.S.R. 968(E) dated 3 November 2026, issued under Section 23(3) read with Section 469, Companies Act, 2013
body: Indian companies looking to raise capital through a direct listing abroad have, until now, been confined to one instrument: the plain equity share. The route itself is fairly young. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs opened it in 2024 through the Companies (Listing of Equity Shares in Permissible Jurisdictions) Rules, letting unlisted Indian companies list equity shares directly on specified stock exchanges outside India, including exchanges in the GIFT City International Financial Services Centre, without first listing in India. A notification dated 3 November 2026, G.S.R. 968(E), now widens that door considerably.

The amendment's drafting technique is almost housekeeping in appearance: wherever the 2024 rules used the word 'shares', the word is now replaced with 'instruments', and the rules themselves are renamed accordingly. But the substance behind that word change is significant. A new definition of 'equity instruments' is inserted, and it covers not just equity shares but convertible debentures and preference shares issued by an Indian company as well. Companies that could previously only send plain equity abroad can now structure an overseas listing around hybrid instruments too, instruments that institutional investors in several permissible jurisdictions are considerably more comfortable pricing and holding than a straight equity stake in an unlisted Indian issuer.

That widening comes with a guardrail. Reporting on the amendment describes a condition tying the expanded route to allocation in favour of Qualified Institutional Buyers, with one account putting the figure at 75 per cent of the offering. The policy logic is not hard to follow: a convertible debenture or preference share is a more complex instrument than an ordinary share, and MCA appears to want sophisticated institutional money, rather than a wider retail-style base, absorbing that complexity in the overseas market before the route is used more freely.

The amendment also replaces Form LEAP-1 in the Second Schedule to the 2024 rules with a revised form, bringing the paperwork in line with the broader category of instruments the rules now cover. Form LEAP-1 is the form through which an Indian company notifies the Registrar of its intention to list, and a form drafted around plain equity shares would have sat awkwardly against a listing built around convertible debentures or preference shares.

What the amendment leaves untouched matters just as much as what it changes. The list of permissible jurisdictions under the 2024 rules, the specific set of overseas stock exchanges an Indian company may list on using this route, has not been expanded by this notification. Commentary on the amendment is also clear that it does not touch the listing regulations of the overseas exchange or the IFSC exchange itself, and does not alter the separate requirements under the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 that govern how foreign investors can hold and trade such instruments. A company planning to use the expanded route still has two different rulebooks to satisfy, the Companies Act framework MCA has just widened, and the FEMA framework that sits alongside it and has not moved.

That gap matters practically because, as some commentary on the amendment points out, the definition of 'equity instruments' inserted into the Companies Act rules is not fully aligned with how the FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Rules define and treat similar instruments. A convertible debenture that qualifies for the new overseas listing route under the Companies Act rules will still need to be checked separately against the FEMA definitions and any sectoral or pricing conditions that apply there, rather than assumed to clear both frameworks on the strength of the Companies Act amendment alone.

For Indian companies weighing an overseas listing, particularly those that had looked at the 2024 route and concluded that straight equity was not the right instrument for their capital structure or investor base, the amendment opens a door that was previously closed. For their counsel and compliance teams, the practical task now is cross-checking any proposed convertible debenture or preference share listing against both the amended Companies Act rules and the unchanged FEMA position, and building the QIB allocation condition into the offer structure from the outset rather than retrofitting it later.
why_it_matters: Companies planning to raise capital abroad, including those backed by foreign private equity or venture investors looking for an exit route through an overseas listing, now have a wider menu of instruments to list directly outside India without a prior domestic listing. The QIB allocation condition and the unchanged FEMA requirements mean the route still needs careful structuring, so promoters and foreign investors weighing an overseas listing should treat this as widening the options, not as removing the compliance work involved in using them.
card_summary: MCA's 3 November 2026 amendment lets Indian companies list convertible debentures and preference shares abroad, not just plain equity shares, with a QIB allocation condition.
card_tip: A debenture or preference-share listing abroad now needs sign-off against both the amended Companies Act rules and the separate, unchanged FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Rules.
verification_notes: The notification number (G.S.R. 968(E)), its date (3 November 2026), and its enacting provisions (Section 23(3) read with Section 469 of the Companies Act, 2013) are corroborated across the Vinod Kothari Consultants, TeamLease RegTech and CorpLawUpdates reports found in this run. The core substantive change (replacement of 'shares' with 'instruments', the new definition of 'equity instruments' covering equity shares, convertible debentures and preference shares, and the Form LEAP-1 replacement) is corroborated across the same sources plus The Week's wire report describing the government as having 'amended direct overseas listing norms for Indian cos'. The 75 per cent QIB allocation figure comes from a Taxscan headline on a related MCA change to the same rules and could not be independently cross-checked against a second outlet in this run; it is reported as given, with that caveat. The unchanged status of the permissible-jurisdictions list and of the FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Rules position is stated in secondary commentary and was not verified against the gazette text, which could not be accessed in this session. This is a regulatory notification, not a court ruling, reported under the news.md scope's provision for regulator circulars with a specific number and date.
